title: Software Evaluation Framework: A Repeatable Way to Choose SaaS
description: A practical software-selection framework with weighted criteria, a pilot scorecard, total-cost calculations, risk checks, and a documented final decision.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Write a Problem Statement and Baseline
sections.body: Describe the workflow that needs to improve, who performs it, how often it occurs, and what currently goes wrong. Record a baseline such as time per task, error or rework rate, missed handoffs, reporting delay, or support burden. Name the person accountable for the decision and the people who will use and administer the system. This prevents the evaluation becoming a feature checklist disconnected from an operational need. Define what success looks like and what would make the purchase unnecessary.

sections.title: Separate Must-Haves From Preferences
sections.body: List mandatory requirements first: legal or security constraints, required integrations, data export, accessibility, deployment needs, and workflows that cannot be interrupted. Eliminate candidates that fail a true must-have before scoring nice-to-have features. Then create weighted criteria for usability, capability, integration effort, reporting, support, scalability, and cost. Choose weights before vendor demos and write down the evidence needed for each score. Do not let a vendor presentation redefine the criteria halfway through the process.

sections.title: Use a Consistent Scorecard
sections.body: Score every candidate against the same criteria on a defined scale—for example, 1 for failing the requirement, 3 for meeting it with a documented workaround, and 5 for meeting it cleanly in the pilot. Multiply each score by its weight and keep evidence next to the number. Mark unknowns as unknown rather than silently awarding an average score. A weighted score organizes the discussion but should not override a failed security requirement, an unacceptable contract term, or a workflow users cannot complete.

sections.title: Run a Task-Based Pilot
sections.body: Choose two or three realistic tasks that cover the main workflow, a handoff, and an exception. Use representative data and ask both a regular user and an administrator to complete them without a vendor guiding every step. Record setup time, completion time, errors, workarounds, permission behavior, export quality, and training required. Test the integration path and one recovery scenario, such as correcting a mistaken record or restoring a previous version. A trial that only tests the easiest path will miss important adoption and operational costs.

sections.title: Calculate Total Cost of Ownership
sections.body: Compare costs over the same period, such as 12 or 36 months. Include subscription fees, minimum seat commitments, usage charges, paid add-ons, implementation, migration, training, administration, integration maintenance, and likely renewal changes. Estimate benefits using your baseline rather than vendor claims: hours plausibly saved, reduced rework, or fewer missed handoffs. State assumptions and run a conservative scenario. Do not treat projected returns as guaranteed or compare one vendor's monthly entry price with another's annual all-in cost.

sections.title: Review Security, Data, and Exit Risks
sections.body: Confirm the access model, administrator controls, audit logs, retention and deletion behavior, export formats, data residency where required, incident notification terms, and current security documentation. Ask who owns configuration and integration credentials, and how access is removed when staff leave. Before purchase, verify that data can be exported in a usable form and identify the steps needed to switch vendors later. Treat unsupported assurances as open questions and assign an owner and due date to each one.

sections.title: Make and Record the Decision
sections.body: Summarize the leading candidate, evidence behind the score, trade-offs accepted, unresolved risks, expected total cost, and conditions under which the recommendation would change. Explain why the runner-up was not selected; that is more useful than declaring a universal winner. Agree on an owner, rollout stages, training, migration checks, and a review date after launch. Revisit the decision when the workflow, team size, security requirements, or pricing changes—not simply because a new tool becomes popular.
